organised workmen of the country who were prac- ticall. unanimous in their aupport of the Bill framed by Mr. Angunit. But, in order to make this point as to the settlement of the amount of competition as clear all possible no will quote the fo lowing palling° from Mr. Cii.te gag- idt IWe speech. I have pointer! me! that one effect of our Bill ID to get rid of litigation. We hese attempted to do that in eeveral ways. In the first place, by the simplicity and the ds finitenesi of our proposals. If a man In Injured In the enures of his employment he b no longer naked he the injury took place. If, however the employer , considers t. at the case is ~ne in which justice will he done by the payment of • wrist, only, or some other , nen, there is proviaion made for the workman and i employer to come to an agreement. If they fail to come tune a gro ement the matter goes at once direct to the county-court judge, who decides without appeal. its to malingering, I think it will be difficult to take place. In the event of that happening the arbitrator, that let.. say the enuntr-dourt judge, would be entitled to call in a Medical man, and upon the statement of that medical man he would decide for how long compeneatlon should be held, sod at the option either of employer or work- man a further application might be made to the medical man n. know whether the workman was still in • cendi- tine which re/gersd compensation. 1 donut think that lee case which will often hsppen."

The debates upon the Bill will no doubt largely turn upon the effect that the measure is likely to have upon the number of accidents. What work- men want is prevention rather than cure. No matter how large or how certain compensation may be it does not make up for the loss of a limb or for any kind of pariaanent disablement. Safe and certain compensation for injuries is a good thing in itself undoubtedly, but if it be secured at the expense of increased negligence in guarding against accidents it may he dearly purchased. Tuesday was a veritable holocaust, and it is all the more sensational owing loth° fact that the bulk of the victims belenged to AM° of the an tat aristocratic families in Franca Although the bazaar was under the petroliage of many of the wealthiest people in Paris it was held in one rf the most ramshackle anti unsuitable buildings it was possible to provide for such an occasion. Ais structure was an 'Ad wooden erection composed of timbur as dry as tinder and with a roof that had been made watertight by the free use of pitch and other inflammable material. Thu building was hung or decorated with a great quantity of cur- tains of light sot fragile material, and its stalls were laden with the articles which are usually found at fashionable hair tars end which were dot- tined to provide reedy fuel for the flames. There were, in addition, mune.ue lumps used for illuminating and decorative purposes. The build- ing was crowded with the elite of Parisian society, there being, it is said, about twelve hundred per. eons present, when suddenly it was snot th.tt sties of the ignitable material had takes fire. There WRY at once a frenzied rush for the doorways. But unfortunately the means of exit lied not boon provided with a view to an emergency of this kind. They were instantly blocked with • struggling inane of hunsamity. Tito “111111.11 in the ineatillieu 11111,1C1 with unparalleled rapidity. to less than five minutes the burning root began to fall on the doomed and helpless vic- tims bel.m. In abort toll or twelves minutes ell wax over, end the scone of the gay gathering of a few mutatee ego was covered with the charred remains of five or six hundred human beingn, for that in the latest estimate of the loss of life, though the official account places the loos at about one hundred and fifty. It is seedless to say that this dresdful tragedy has excited a world-wide sympathy. What etrikee an English reader, in considering the cause of the calamity, is the extraordinery went of municipal control. It is impossible to believe that losal authorities in thie country would permit a bees., Cr any other gathering at which there was a dan- ger of tire, to be held in such a building es that which has been burned to the ground et Paris. The need for the fullest precautions in guarding against contlegrations is certainly the main Name to be derived from this latest disaster as it bee been that of so many which have preceded it.

At the meeting of the Rural District Council on Wednesday the Surveyor (Mr. Owen) re- ported upon two separate sewerage schemes for connecting Nitwit° with the Corporation sewers, against both of which serious objections may be raised—in cue case on the ground of inefficiency and in the other on that of cost. In regard to the tiret and cheapest scheme, Mr. Owen exgrmem • doubt whethen the Local Oavernment Board would approve it owing to the very slight fall it allows. The Warrington Trades and Laboor Council had the benefit lut week of a lecture upon bi-metalliete, which is no doubt a very important goestion, and certainly a very &Baruse one in some site upects. Unfortenately lecturers upon the sub- ject, even when addreeeing working class audiences, do not enter as fully as they might do into what may be described as the wage-earners ' side of bi- metallism. The lecturer of Tuesday pointed out that twice as many commodities here now to be sold in order to obtain • given quan- tity of money as woe the case t weety-fi years goo. But then wage-earners—that is practi- cally the whole 1111114 of working people—do not sell commodities for money but buy com- modities with money. They are paid their wants Its money and they expend those warm in the par- chew of the neceeeartes and itome of the luxuries of life. If, then, by the adoption of hi-metalliste the prii ref thews necessaries and luxuries were raised to the onset of 23 per cent, it is evident that there would be an eguivnent re Noting in the purchasing power of wane.. In other words, it would IN qirel two pounds to purchase what can new be obtained for thirty shillings. There is no doubt a good deal to be mid for bi-metallitm but until its advocates can convince the working class°s that it would not mesa a wholesale reduttion in the purchuing power of Ingo there is not muclo chance of it. adoption in this country.
